senses.definition: Any of various knots used to attach a rope to an object other than another rope.
A fastener or connection point, as for a trailer.
examples: His truck sported a heavy-duty hitch for his boat.

senses.definition: (informal) A problem, delay or source of difficulty.
examples: The banquet went off without a hitch

quotes.text: The service operated according to plan on the Monday morning with only a few hitches.
quotes.reference: 1961 July, “Glasgow emergency - the restoration of Clydeside steam suburban services”, in Trains Illustrated, page 432:

quotes.text: Over the next week, the hitch in my dad's stride eased a bit. But we'd run out of things to talk about.
quotes.reference: 2008 October, Davy Rothbart, “How I caught up with dad”, in Men's Health, volume 23, number 8, →ISSN, page 110:

senses.definition: A hidden or unfavorable condition or element.
examples: The deal sounds too good to be true. What's the hitch?

senses.definition: (military, slang) A period of time spent in the military.
examples: She served two hitches in Vietnam.
U.S. TROOPS FACE LONGER ARMY HITCH; SOLDIERS BOUND FOR IRAQ, ... WILL BE RETAINED

senses.definition: A large Californian minnow, Lavinia exilicauda.
(mining) A hole cut into the wall of a mine on which timbers are rested.
examples: A coal cutter and conveyor is used along the face, and after each cut the hitch had to be crossed at a new point.

quotes.text: An upcast fault is when the seam is thrown up; to counteract this a "canch" of top stone must be taken down outbye over from the fault, and a "canch" of bottom stone taken up inbye over from the fault, then level up to the bottom of your "canch" at the foreside of the hitch outbye over until you have a regular gradient to the seam on the hitch.
quotes.reference: 1879, William Bailes, Student's Guide to the Principles of Coal & Metal Mining, page 17:

examples: She hitched her jeans up and then tightened her belt.
He hitched the bedroll to his backpack and went camping.

quotes.text: Philander went into the next room, which was just a lean-to hitched on to the end of the shanty, and came back with a salt mackerel that dripped brine like a rainstorm. Then he put the coffee pot on the stove and rummaged out a loaf of dry bread and some hardtack.
quotes.reference: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter VIII, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y.; London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:

quotes.text: The company has hitched its future to artificial intelligence — whether with its voice-enabled digital assistant or its automated placement of advertising for marketers — as the breakthrough technology to make the next generation of services and devices smarter and more capable.

senses.definition: (informal) To marry oneself to; especially to get hitched.
(informal, transitive) Clipping of hitchhike, to thumb a ride.
(intransitive) To become entangled or caught; to be linked or yoked; to unite; to cling.

senses.definition: (intransitive) To move interruptedly or with halts, jerks, or steps; said of something obstructed or impeded.
examples: Frank’s breath hitched in his throat when he saw the knife being pointed at him.

quotes.text: To ease themselves […] by hitching into another place.
